subject: Zakaria: Blue Cities in Blue States Largely Have the Worst Homelessness Problems
posts:
When urban housing costs and homelessness surge, commentators point fingers at blue-state governance.
Evidence: High budgets, strict housing caps, urban crisis
#Aletheia #UrbanPolicy #Housing

Fareed Zakaria argues that blue cities face acute homelessness because of over-regulating housing and overprivileging homeless rights over the public.
Stated Judgement: (+0.8, +0.5) — Trustworthy Good

While spending and zoning friction are real, framing complex housing failures strictly as partisan municipal failure ignores broader macroeconomic and federal safety net gaps.
Resulting Judgement: (-0.4, -0.3) — Lesser Evil

Verdict: COND — The Path of Redemption.
Analysis links local zoning rigidity to real crises, but partisan finger-pointing obscures systemic housing deficits.

Integrity: Conditionally Sound (Hypocrisy: 1.6, z: 1)

Sub-Audits Breakdown:
- Fareed Zakaria: COND (0.8, 0.5) — Highlights zoning failures but frames via partisan lens.
- Urban Housing Policy: COND (-0.4, -0.3) — Conflates local spending with systemic market failure.
CNN host Fareed Zakaria highlighted that major blue cities grapple with severe homelessness despite heavy spending, pointing to strict building restrictions.

The Bright Side:
It forces a candid debate on zoning reform and municipal fiscal efficiency.

The Breakdown & Plane Error:
Conflating WHO (municipal leadership) with WHAT (structural zoning and housing supply failure), leading to partisan deflection.

Social Physics Analysis:
Zakaria runs a partial Smart Selfish maneuver, using real municipal inefficiencies as a pretext to project systemic housing policy failures onto progressive governance models.

The Trajectory: The Path of Redemption.
When you map the gap between political rhetoric and housing reality, it plots a direct trajectory toward Redemption through necessary zoning reform.

The Unavoidable Truth: Restrictive zoning and high costs drive acute urban homelessness.
The Unavoidable Lie: Partisan municipal mismanagement is the sole root cause.

Alethekanon:
Pointing out municipal spending flaws is fair, but ignoring macro housing economics turns critique into partisan theater.

Awwthekanon:
Every unhoused neighbor represents a housing market failure that deserves compassion and concrete building solutions, not political point-scoring.

Brothekanon:
Classic cable news take—blaming blue mayors for expensive housing misses how hard it is to build anywhere in this country.

Spirithekanon:
"Better is a handful with quietness than both hands full together with toil and chasing of the wind." Ecclesiastes 4:6 PASS
True urban flourishing requires balanced stewardship rather than endless political shouting matches.

The post Zakaria: Blue Cities in Blue States Largely Have the Worst Homelessness Problems appeared first on Breitbart.

Actual Article Body:
On Friday’s broadcast of HBO’s “Real Time,” CNN host and Washington Post columnist Fareed Zakaria said that the cities with “the most acute homelessness problems…are blue cities in blue states, to a large extent.”

Zakaria said, “Let me say something that’s going to get me into trouble, which is, if you look at where you have the most acute homelessness problems, they are blue cities in blue states, to a large extent. … And what you have is a situation where Anand is absolutely right that the right tends to be very stingy about the money that it would take to solve these problems. But that’s not New York City, that’s not L.A. We’re spending crazy amounts of money on it, but there is this other side to it, … which is the great, in my view, it’s sort of — it’s overprivileging the rights of the homeless over the rights of the other 99.5%.”

He added, “[W]hen you look at cities, it’s not happening in all cities. … Miami does not have the kind of homelessness problem that New York has. Houston doesn’t, Dallas doesn’t. Part of it is that those places are much better at building stuff. One of the problems in a place like New York or in California is we just can’t build housing, of any kind, right? Affordable, homeless, whatever it is, and people don’t want it. And so, part of the issue here, as I say, the tragedy is, it is happening in some cities, it is not happening in all cities.”

Author Anand Giridharadas responded that homeless people don’t stay in places that treat them poorly, which Zakaria said doesn’t seem fair to him, but he doesn’t know enough to say so definitively. Zakaria reiterated that part of the issue is the ability or inability to build.
